variants.title: Read the state
variants.context: Accepted means the service durably owns authorized ciphertext delivery work. Device delivered means one named recipient device persisted and acknowledged its envelope. Read is a later recipient event. Pending means at least one device lacks an acknowledgement. Expired means the bounded queue stops retrying; it does not imply delivery.
variants.prompt: A recipient has two devices; one acknowledged, one has not. What is the message’s state?
options: Delivered, because a recipient device acknowledged it.
Read, because an acknowledgement arrived from a device.
Pending, because one device still lacks an acknowledgement.
optionFeedback: One device acknowledging does not make the message delivered to the recipient.
An acknowledgement records receipt on a device; reading is a separate later event.
Delivery state is per device.
variants.explanation: Expose sent, device-delivered, and read as separate evidence.

variants.prompt: An undelivered ciphertext envelope reaches the end of its retention. Which state, and what does it imply?
options: Read, because the queue only clears once a device consumes it.
Expired, and the server stops retrying without delivering.
Delivered, because retention only ends after a handoff.
optionFeedback: The queue clears on a retention deadline, not on a recipient action.
Expiry is a retention decision, not a delivery event.
Retention ends on a timer; no handoff to a device took place.
variants.explanation: Expire undelivered ciphertext according to an explicit retention contract.

variants.prompt: When may the sender see accepted?
options: When the recipient opens and reads the message.
After authorized encrypted work is durable and replayable.
As soon as the gateway receives the frame.
optionFeedback: Reading happens much later, and it may never happen at all.
Acceptance follows durable ciphertext acceptance.
A frame at the gateway is not yet durable or replayable.
variants.explanation: Acknowledge acceptance only after durable, replayable work.

variants.title: Assign the owner
variants.context: Client devices own content keys, encryption, and seen-message IDs. Gateways own socket lifecycle and location, not history. The conversation service owns membership, idempotency, and conversation-local order. The delivery plane owns per-device envelopes, retries, and expiry. Routing services never receive keys.
variants.prompt: A routing service asks for content keys to repair a stuck delivery. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, because repair work is a narrow exception.
Only decryption keys are sensitive, so sending others is fine.
Content keys stay on client devices and never reach routing.
optionFeedback: A repair path is still a path, and the trust model has no exception for it.
Any content key hands the service plaintext, whichever way it is used.
Plaintext and keys stay outside routing, queue, and storage services.
variants.explanation: Keep plaintext and content keys outside the service.

variants.prompt: A gateway process stores conversation history to speed up reconnects. What is wrong?
options: The gateway should cache the content keys alongside it.
Gateways own socket lifecycle and location, not history.
Nothing is wrong; a reconnect cache is a fair optimization.
optionFeedback: Adding keys to a server makes it worse; keys stay on client devices.
Connection gateways must not become history authorities.
A gateway can be replaced at any moment, so history cached there is not durable.
variants.hint: What is the replay source of truth?
variants.explanation: The message log and outbox own durable acceptance and replay.

variants.prompt: Which component assigns conversation-local order and enforces sender idempotency?

The conversation service.

optionFeedback: Media is a separate plane and never orders conversation messages.
Membership, idempotency, and sequence are the conversation service’s job.
Gateways authenticate and locate devices; they assign no order.

variants.title: Trace private delivery
variants.context: The path: the client encrypts one authenticated envelope per target device; the gateway authenticates and assigns conversation-local order; ciphertext metadata and per-device delivery events are committed before acknowledging; delivery pushes to online sessions, retains bounded work for offline devices, and completes only the acknowledging device record.
variants.prompt: A user sends a message to a friend with two devices. Put the path in order.

items.text: The gateway authenticates the session, enforces limits, authorizes membership, and assigns conversation-local order.
Delivery pushes to online sessions, retains bounded work for offline devices, and completes only the acknowledging device’s record.
The client creates one message ID, resolves recipient device sessions, and encrypts one envelope per target device.
Ciphertext metadata and per-device delivery events are committed before acknowledging acceptance.

variants.hint: Per-device envelopes exist before the service sees anything.
variants.explanation: The sender acknowledgement follows durable ciphertext acceptance; delivery is later and per device.

items.text: No new commit is created; the existing delivery events stand.
The client resends the same message ID and envelopes.

variants.title: Hold the invariant
variants.context: One logical message keeps one stable identity, remains encrypted while the service handles it, and has independent delivery state per recipient device. Retries may repeat transport work but never the visible message; one device’s acknowledgement never erases another device’s pending copy.
variants.prompt: Device A acknowledges; device B’s pending envelope is deleted as a result. What was violated?
options: Independent delivery state: one device must not clear another.
Nothing; one acknowledgement settles the message for the user.
Encryption, since deleting an envelope exposes its ciphertext.
optionFeedback: Each device has its own delivery state.
Device B never receives the message, so the user loses it on that device.
Deleting an envelope reveals nothing; the broken rule is per-device state.
variants.hint: How many delivery states does one message have?
variants.explanation: Independent delivery state for every recipient device.

variants.prompt: May the service store plaintext briefly for spam scanning?
options: Yes, as long as only gateway processes hold it.
No; the message stays encrypted while the service handles it.
Yes, if the plaintext is discarded within seconds.
optionFeedback: A gateway is still the service, and it never holds plaintext.
The router cannot assume access to plaintext.
A short window is still a window in which the service can read messages.
variants.explanation: Privacy-compatible metadata controls and reports, not plaintext.

variants.prompt: Why can retries repeat transport work safely?

Because messages are small enough that duplicates are cheap.
Because one logical message keeps one stable identity.
optionFeedback: Retries exist precisely because the network drops and repeats frames.
Cheap duplicates are still duplicates the recipient would see twice.
Stable identity plus durable seen-message IDs on devices.
